lesson.title: Before You Test: Checking the Fine Print
lesson.summary: A one-proportion z-test is only trustworthy when the sample is random, the observations are independent, and the sample is large enough for the null sampling distribution to be approximately normal.
lesson.body:
The one-proportion z-test relies on the sampling distribution of phat being approximately normal, which is only guaranteed under certain conditions. There are three conditions to check before trusting the p-value from a z-test. First, randomness: the data must come from a random sample or a randomized experiment, so that the results can be generalized and are not distorted by selection bias. Second, independence: individual observations need to be roughly independent of each other. When sampling without replacement from a finite population, this is checked with the 10 percent condition, the sample size n should be no more than 10 percent of the population size N, so that removing sampled individuals does not meaningfully change the probabilities for the ones remaining. Third, the Large Counts condition, sometimes called the success or failure condition: both np0 and n(1 - p0) must be at least 10. This is the same idea behind checking the standard deviation of a sample proportion, it guarantees the binomial sampling distribution of phat is close enough to a normal curve that z-procedures give trustworthy results.

Notice that, just like the test statistic itself, the Large Counts condition for a test uses p0, the null hypothesis value, not phat. This makes sense: you are checking whether the sampling distribution assumed under H0 is approximately normal, and that sampling distribution is centered at p0. A confidence interval, by contrast, has no null hypothesis to lean on, so its version of this condition checks n(phat) and n(1 - phat) instead.

Check these conditions against the customer satisfaction example from the previous section. Randomness: the consumer group sampled customers at random, so that condition is met. Independence: as long as the company has at least 1,500 customers total, 10 times the sample size of 150, the 10 percent condition is satisfied. Large Counts: np0 = 150(0.70) = 105 and n(1 - p0) = 150(0.30) = 45, and both are comfortably at least 10. All three conditions check out, so the z-test and its p-value of about 0.016 from the previous section can be trusted.

When any of these conditions is not met, most seriously a small np0 or n(1 - p0), the normal approximation can break down and the p-value from a z-test is no longer reliable. Checking conditions is not a box-ticking formality, it is what separates a test statistic from a trustworthy conclusion. The same three-condition habit, randomness, independence, and a large-counts-style check, carries over almost unchanged to the test for two proportions covered next, and to the t-procedures covered later in this unit.
